Note on the Goold-Verschoyle family.

Mrs. Sybil M. Goold-Verschoyle (mentioned inter alia at 42a) is the mother of five children who were brought up at the family home the Manor House, Dunkineely, Co. Donegal. I believe that the eldest is:-

Sheila, whose married name is FitzGerald. I understand that, at one time she and her husband kept a guest house in Eire, but subsequently she moved to Winchester, where I believe she is managing the local branch of Culpeper House. I have been given to understand that the guest house venture failed owing to the fact that greater attention was given to the well-being of the large assortment of dogs kept by the family than to the guests. This is undoubtedly the Sheila referred to at 37a. I have never met her.

The second daughter Eileen Goold-Verschoyle married about the year 1933, Gerald Simms, the eldest son of J.F.A. Simms and Mrs. Simms of Combermore, Lifford, Co. Donegal. J.F.A. Simms was at the time Crown prosecutor for Co. Tyrone and the agent for the Duke of Abercorn. Mrs. Simms, whose maiden name was Stanger is the daughter of a naturalised German. During the 1914/18 war she was subjected to certain restrictions. Gerald Simms is a brilliant scholar, was educated at Winchester and Balliol College, Oxford and is, apparently a successful administrator in the I.C.S. He is extremely well balanced and possessed of unusually great common sense, though his original turns both of thought and conversation may sometimes give the contrary impression. Sheila is intelligent but has strong political leanings to the Left. Her sympathies are probably more with the Trotsky group than the ruling group in Russia at the present time. Her opinions are probably based mainly on emotion and she is in other ways extremely unconventional. She has four children and intends that they should be educated at national, i.e. State subsidised schools, and they are at present allowed a great deal of freedom, as she believes in the Montessori method of training. Possibly her lack of orthodoxy and her husband's common sense are best illustrated by the fact that, when living in the English community in India, she insisted upon having the native doctor to attend her confinement. She would probably have preferred this in any event to illustrate her attitude towards the colour question; her husband permitted this on the grounds that the local native doctor was an abler man than the local English doctor.

Dennis (or Denis) Goold-Verschoyle is I believe, farming in South Africa at the moment. He was an extreme Irish Nationalist. He spoke gaelic in preference to English and both he and

Brian Goold-Verschoyle (mentioned inter alia at 28a) refused to meet a party of which I was a member, when we were invited to tea at the Manor House in 1933. With the exception of myself, the party consisted entirely of relatives, and I understood at the time that the reason that Brian and Denis did not appear was a) that I was an Englishman and b) that another member of the party, although an Irishman was at the time a commissioned officer in the British Army.

The remaining son, Neil (the subject of P.F. 41426) is the one with whom I am the best acquainted. He appeared to me to be the best balanced of the family, as he could be relied upon to behave normally in any usual social setting. He came to London in about 1934 and was employed at the B.B.C and I met him on various occasions at the B.B.C. athletic grounds, and at the house of Gerald Simms's cousins the Rectory, 73 Gloucester Place, W.1.
